situations.name: Settings panel scaffold
situations.definition: A developer adding a new settings tab needs the canonical multi-section panel shape: header, quick-nav rail, section cards, scroll-spy.
situations.note: Only 6 of 13 lazy-loaded settings tabs use SettingsScaffold; the rest hand-roll ContentBox + SectionCard stacks or a SegmentedTabs strip, so nav affordance and section typography differ per tab.

situations.name: Preference persistence
situations.definition: A developer adding a user-facing setting must decide where the value lives and how it survives restart.
situations.note: Three unrelated backends coexist: DB-backed `useAppSetting` (with a validator + debounce-race comment), zustand `persist` for the theme store, and a module-level telemetry preference file. Nothing tells the next author which to pick.

situations.name: View-state memory
situations.definition: A developer wants a surface to remember the user's last filter, panel width, board scope, or dismissed hint across navigation and restart.
situations.note: Every surface invents its own `personas.<feature>.<thing>` localStorage key and its own lazy-init + write-back pair; only Mastermind graduated to a versioned DB doc, and it had to write a one-time migration off the legacy keys to do it.

situations.name: Guided tour authoring
situations.definition: A developer adding a feature wants an in-app tour step that navigates to it, spotlights it, and completes when the user actually does the thing.
situations.note: Converged on one engine but the per-step side effects are a hardcoded `else if (step.id === …)` ladder in GuidedTour and the nav sub-tab setters are a fixed list of seven — every new step edits four files, which the README documents rather than fixes.

situations.name: First-run onboarding flow
situations.definition: A developer needs a gated multi-step first-launch sequence that lands the user on a working artifact.
situations.note: One implementation, but the step state machine, per-step async load phases, double-click dedupe and retry paths all live in one 359-line hook — and the overlay/tour precedence contract lives in prose, not code.

situations.name: First-use consent gate
situations.definition: A developer needs a blocking acceptance the user must give once before the app is usable, plus a way to inspect and reset it.
situations.note: Consent is stored in localStorage and reset by a settings button that then asks the user to reload — a hard reset path with no audit trail, and the modal is the only surface that can re-collect it.

situations.name: Impact-disclosure gate
situations.definition: Before a click spawns an agent that can write to the user's repo, the developer needs a gate that states impact class, ordered steps, and boundaries.
situations.note: A genuinely good primitive (impact hue, fact strip, 'what it will not do' list) that only the passport wall uses; every other agent-spawning door in the slice — Mastermind, Studio autonomous mode, SkillsWorkbench quick tiles — dispatches with no disclosure at all. The catalog's honesty depends on a code comment asking authors to keep prose and code in sync.

situations.name: Destructive-action confirmation
situations.definition: A developer needs a delete / disband / revoke / reset action to be hard to trigger by accident and easy to undo the intent of.
situations.note: Five incompatible idioms in one slice: arm-on-first-click hook, popover InlineConfirm with click-outside, shared ConfirmDialog modal, local `confirmXId` + 3.5s timeout, and an arm-DELAY (450ms) that disables the button instead of arming it. The safety level a user gets depends on which file they are in.

situations.name: Workspace export selection
situations.definition: A developer needs the user to pick exactly which entities leave the machine in a portable bundle.
situations.note: Two full implementations ship side by side (the modal and the 'export-prototype' scope-rail/manifest-cart), the inventory hook fans out to nine independent list APIs, and truncation warnings arrive as free-text strings the UI just prints.

situations.name: Import conflict resolution
situations.definition: A developer needs the user to rule on incoming items that collide with existing local data, per row.
situations.note: The panel's own comment says it 'mirrors the credential conflict card' — i.e. the same skip/duplicate/replace decision is implemented twice with different vocabularies (`keep_both` vs `duplicate`), and the two-pass import contract lives only in comments.

situations.name: Passphrase-gated secret transfer
situations.definition: A developer needs credentials to leave or enter the vault only behind a user-supplied passphrase, with the encrypted blob never leaking to disk unprotected.
situations.note: The passphrase is threaded through as raw props on a 15-prop component rather than owned by a gate primitive; the only enforcement of the gate is one test file.

situations.name: Sensitive clipboard handling
situations.definition: A developer needs to hand the user a secret (bundle bytes, share link, plaintext key) via the clipboard without leaving it there.
situations.note: Only BundleExportDialog implements a verify-then-wipe TTL (and had to reason about the force-wipe branch when the read fails); every other copy path uses the plain shared copy helper with no expiry.

situations.name: One-time secret reveal
situations.definition: A developer needs to display a value that exists exactly once (a minted key, a pairing code) and can never be re-fetched.
situations.note: Each dialog re-decides how loudly to say 'this will not be shown again' and whether closing is guarded; getting it wrong is unrecoverable for the user.

situations.name: Device pairing ceremony
situations.definition: A developer needs a two-sided handshake between machines that survives event loss, is testable, and explains every refusal.
situations.note: Best-factored flow in the slice (pure machine, event and poll paths share one transition, typed refusal codes); backend owns the other half in engine/src/p2p/device_pairing.rs. Refusal codes are recovered by string-matching Rust error messages, so a backend rewording silently degrades to `unknown`. A SECOND unrelated 'pairing' (cloud-app key minting) shares the word.

situations.name: Scoped capability grant
situations.definition: A developer needs the user to mint a least-privilege, time-boxed token for an external caller.
situations.note: Scope vocabulary (`personas:execute:persona:<id>`) is hand-built in two dialogs; the approval modal re-declares its own scope set and expiry options rather than importing the create dialog's.

situations.name: Connector slot binding
situations.definition: A developer needs a UI where the user declares which vault credential backs a given capability, environment, or project slot.
situations.note: The detected-vs-bound distinction (evidence about the code vs the operator's declaration) is a real conceptual win that only EnvConnectorSlot models; the others collapse it. Service-type allow-lists are duplicated as literal string arrays in at least three files.

situations.name: Agent session dispatch
situations.definition: A developer wants a button that spawns a Claude/Fleet session in some repo and keeps it addressable afterwards.
situations.note: Four dispatch idioms coexist: raw `spawnSession`, keyed `dispatchRowToFleet` (with a one-session-per-key guard), `dispatchSkillToRepo` (install-then-invoke, memory + reflection blocks appended), and the universal DispatchChooserModal. Only the keyed path prevents a double-spawn; only the skill path guarantees the slash command resolves.

situations.name: Agent briefing composition
situations.definition: A developer needs to turn app state into a prompt/context block a dispatched agent can trust, without leaking secrets.
situations.note: Every briefing is string concatenation with its own 'credential VALUES never leave the vault' discipline restated in a comment. The redaction rule (an allow-list Set of connector service types) exists in exactly one file and is not enforced anywhere else.

situations.name: Live session terminal
situations.definition: A developer needs to show a running agent session's output inside a feature surface and let the user reply to it.
situations.note: PassportTerminalModal's header comment says it lifted Mastermind's composition into a BaseModal — a copy, not an extraction; the reply row, the liveness predicate and the 'headless / gone' copy are duplicated.

situations.name: Proposal review queue
situations.definition: A developer needs a surface where a human accepts, adjusts, or rejects machine-generated proposals one at a time.
situations.note: rowWrites exists precisely because 15 call sites swallowed failed verdict writes — yet both KPI proposal queues in this slice still write through `updateKpi` directly, outside the compare-and-swap door. Two of the seven surfaces decide the SAME rows with different layouts, and PolicyProposalsSection needed a 20-line comment to justify not merging.

situations.name: Generate-preview-apply
situations.definition: A developer wants the user to describe intent, have an LLM draft a structure, review it, and commit it.
situations.note: Each re-invents the phase enum (`idle | previewing | applying` vs `type | pick | compose | verify` vs `scaffolding | starting | live | error`), the keyboard affordances, and whether the composed artifact is frozen and replayed or re-composed on every run.

situations.name: Long-running job progress
situations.definition: A developer kicks off a backend scan/build/measurement that takes seconds to minutes and must show progress, survive unmount, and end cleanly.
situations.note: Poll intervals are per-file magic numbers (1500 / 5000 / 6000 / 30000 ms); cancellation is variously an `alive` local, an `aliveRef`, a `cancelled` closure flag, or nothing. Studio needed a second 'liveness watch' loop because the boot poll stopped at first success and nothing noticed the server dying.

situations.name: Streaming output rendering
situations.definition: A developer needs to render a token-by-token agent stream without re-rendering the whole surface per chunk.
situations.note: Studio solved it twice (rAF-coalesced store commits AND a narrow `useShallow` selector) with the reasoning captured only in comments; the team channel solves the adjacent problem with refcounted subscriptions instead. No shared primitive.

situations.name: Backend event subscription
situations.definition: A developer needs a component or hook to react to a Tauri backend event and refresh the right slice of state.
situations.note: A `useTauriEvent` hook exists, but most listeners are hand-rolled `listen(...).then(u => …)` with a `cancelled` flag guarding the async unlisten race — the same eight-line boilerplate repeated, and each re-decides whether a missed event needs a recovery poll.

situations.name: Infinite canvas surface
situations.definition: A developer needs a pannable/zoomable spatial board with draggable nodes, links, and overlays.
situations.note: The worst divergence in the slice: a hand-rolled SVG camera with render-free panning and rAF-coalesced zoom (Mastermind), an @xyflow/react graph with a 27-action reducer (sub_canvas, now DEAD — TeamCanvas.tsx documents it as orphaned), a bespoke foreignObject SVG graph (PresetConnectionGraph), and the shared KanbanBoard. Three of these solve node-drag independently.

situations.name: Layout document persistence
situations.definition: A developer needs spatial/board layout to survive restart, tolerate two writers, and migrate as the schema evolves.
situations.note: Solved once, thoroughly — versioned doc, debounced write-through, one-time legacy migration, IPC-unavailable fallback, per-object `author` so an agent's edits can be reverted without touching the user's. Nothing else in the app reuses any of it, and the pattern is exactly what the scattered localStorage keys need.

situations.name: Derived-state publication
situations.definition: A developer needs frontend-derived state that no backend query can reproduce to be readable by an agent or another surface.
situations.note: Low recurrence, high consequence: its rule 1 is 'never publish the demo scene' — the failure mode is an agent confidently describing six projects that do not exist. The camelCase contract must be kept in lockstep with a Rust struct by hand.

situations.name: Member roster & capabilities
situations.definition: A developer needs a list of team members with their roles/capabilities and per-member toggles.
situations.note: Three roster renderings (split studio, preset studio, dead canvas) each define their own member view-model; presence (`working`/`waiting`) is derived in a fourth place from the channel step layer with a 10-minute staleness bound that only that file knows about.

situations.name: Entity creation form
situations.definition: A developer needs a create form with inline name-uniqueness feedback, validation gates, and side-effect provisioning on submit.
situations.note: The shared availability/validation primitives are good, but the side effect on submit (TeamList provisions a Codebase credential after `createTeam` and toasts on failure without rolling back) has no pattern — a half-created entity is the default failure mode.

situations.name: Tier / build gating
situations.definition: A developer needs a feature to appear only for a given audience tier or build flavour.
situations.note: One clean primitive, but the compile-time axis (`VITE_APP_TIER` tree-shaking) and the runtime axis (user switch) are conflated, and a deprecated `VIEW_MODES` alias layer still ships. Consumers duplicate the same `isStarter ? tourA : tourB` branch rather than declaring a gate.

situations.name: Status vocabulary mapping
situations.definition: A developer needs to turn a backend status token into a label, colour, and icon consistently.
situations.note: At least 30 local `Record<Token, {label,color,icon}>` maps across the slice. `tokenLabel()` from tokenMaps is the sanctioned door but is used in only 5 places; the rest hardcode English labels (157 literal `label: '…'` occurrences in sub_factory alone), which is simultaneously a design-consistency and an i18n-compliance defect.

situations.name: Settings change audit
situations.definition: A developer changing a setting needs the change recorded and surfaced back to the user as history.
situations.note: Only 3 of 13 settings tabs render the chip, and the component's own doc admits categories exist that have no write site yet — the audit trail silently omits the tabs that matter most (api keys aside: engine, byom, network, devices, portability all write without auditing).

situations.name: Search-entry contribution
situations.definition: A developer wants their feature's toggles and destinations reachable from the global command palette.
situations.note: Explicitly documented as 'the reference implementation of the search-entry provider pattern' and explicitly awaiting siblings — the pattern exists but no second domain has adopted it, so teams/studio/onboarding contribute nothing to search.

situations.name: Unsaved-changes guard
situations.definition: A developer needs to stop a user navigating away from a dirty editor without a save/discard decision.
situations.note: A shared hook exists and exactly one surface uses it; TeamStudioSplitVariant re-implements the same thing as a `pendingNav` state + ConfirmDialog, and the Factory's KPI `edits` map is dirty state with no guard at all.

situations.name: Cross-feature deep link
situations.definition: A developer wants a click in one module to open another module focused on a specific entity.
situations.note: The consume-once-then-clear idiom is consistent, but each destination adds a bespoke `pendingXFocus` slot to the global store, and the read happens in a mount effect — a destination that is already mounted misses the handoff.

situations.name: Demo data disclosure
situations.definition: A developer needs a surface to be explorable before real data exists without the user mistaking samples for their own data.
situations.note: Mastermind handles it well (visible notice, corner badge, and a hard rule that demo scenes are never published to Athena). The dead canvas debugger and the Factory's `Mock*` type names show the same idea without the disclosure — mock and real share the renderer with nothing marking which is which.

situations.name: Partial-failure disclosure
situations.definition: A developer needs a surface that fetches several independent data families to say which ones failed instead of rendering a silent partial truth.
situations.note: The strongest instances (DataHealthBar; onboarding's explicit `loading|loaded|empty|error` + `trending|fallback` source phases) both had to be retrofitted after a silent-partial bug. Most other multi-fetch surfaces still collapse failure into an empty list.

situations.name: Drill-down shell
situations.definition: A developer needs a multi-level navigation surface (wall to project to group to detail) with breadcrumbs and preserved sub-tab state.
situations.note: Solved once and well (tab state lifted above the project-keyed subtree so a project switch does not drop you back to Overview) — but only the Factory has it; Teams and Settings hand-roll their own two-level selection.

situations.name: In-page tab strip
situations.definition: A developer needs to switch between sibling views inside a page.
situations.note: SegmentedTabs is used 6 times; Factory, Studio, Ship and the passport wall each hand-roll a strip (wallConfig even ships its own SORT_TABS/VIEW_TABS spec type).

situations.name: Comparison matrix grid
situations.definition: A developer needs a dense entity x dimension grid where cells carry status ink and open per-cell actions.
situations.note: The ink vocabulary (colour only in text and thin bars, healthy values recede, unwired reads as a blue invitation) is a genuine design system that lives in one feature and is explicitly noted as not yet adopted by the cockpit bench that inspired it.

situations.name: Shipped design variants
situations.definition: A developer explores several UI directions for one surface and needs to keep them switchable in the product while the winner is chosen.
situations.note: There is no retirement ritual: the whole sub_canvas tree (29 files, a 27-action reducer, an optimizer, a dry-run debugger) is documented as orphaned in TeamCanvas.tsx and still ships; 'export-prototype' and the losing studio variants likewise.

situations.name: Theme customization
situations.definition: A developer needs the user to author a custom colour theme and know whether the result is readable.
situations.note: Live WCAG contrast readout on three key pairs is the right shape; the concern is that the derived-var pipeline duplicates knowledge of which CSS variables matter, so a new token silently escapes the contrast check.

situations.name: Tables
situations.definition: A developer needs a data table with loading, empty, and row-entrance behaviour.
situations.note: Documented elsewhere. In this slice UnifiedTable is used twice; ~8 surfaces hand-roll `grid-cols-[…]` headers plus their own CASCADE_ROWS / ghost-row logic.

situations.name: Modals
situations.definition: A developer needs a focus-trapped overlay dialog.
situations.note: Documented elsewhere. Worth flagging: two import paths for the same primitive coexist in the slice (`@/lib/ui/BaseModal` 17x, `@/features/shared/components/modals` 9x).

situations.name: Page loading choreography
situations.definition: A developer needs a cold-load sequence that never flashes empty and never hides rendered rows.
situations.note: Documented elsewhere. Well adopted here (module-scoped caches, id-guarded cascades); the outlier is SettingsPage's bespoke idle-unmount sweep, which is a memory strategy layered on top of the loading contract.
